paragraphs: Estimating a causal effect becomes difficult when hidden factors influence both treatments and outcomes. Proxy variables can help represent those hidden influences, but researchers usually need background knowledge to justify which proxies are valid. This paper investigates how to select them from data when several treatments and one outcome share unmeasured confounders.

The approach works within a linear causal model. It first extends an existing proxy estimator from one hidden confounder to multiple hidden confounders. It then develops two sets of conditions under which valid proxies can be identified: one uses second-order statistics, while the other uses higher-order statistics. These conditions support two methods that select proxies and estimate causal effects without bias.

The authors provide theoretical arguments for their algorithms and report supporting experiments on synthetic and real-world data. The contribution is a route toward automating a choice previously justified through subject knowledge. Its guarantees remain tied to the linear setting and the stated identifiability conditions.
icml-2024-automating-the-selection-of-pr.tldr: The paper develops methods to select valid proxies for multiple hidden confounders and estimate causal effects under explicit linear-model identifiability conditions.

paragraphs: Active domain adaptation improves a model in a new domain by choosing a small number of examples for annotation. An overall improvement can conceal uneven progress: categories that are easy to improve may receive most of the benefit, while difficult categories remain poorly recognized. This paper makes the category needing improvement an explicit part of the selection problem.

The method identifies unlabeled examples that matter most for recognizing a targeted category. It uses an influence function to assess how each example affects recognition loss on target-domain data. This gives the selection procedure a direct connection to the prediction objective, rather than relying on an indirect measure of which examples might be useful.

Experiments across three datasets support the method's effectiveness for category-aware adaptation. The intended benefit is more deliberate allocation of a limited annotation effort, with the aim of improving an individual category without harming others. The reported evidence supports that approach; the abstract does not present the no-harm objective as a universal guarantee.
icml-2024-category-aware-active-domain-a.tldr: The method uses influence estimates to choose target-domain examples for annotation that support recognition of a particular category.

paragraphs: Consistency models can produce high-quality images in few generation steps, making them attractive for interactive visual creation. This paper asks how to add controls such as sketches, depth, or poses to pretrained models. It studies ControlNet as a way to supply those additional conditions while retaining the generative capabilities of consistency models.

The authors first find that a ControlNet trained for diffusion models can transfer directly to consistency models for broad semantic control. However, that transfer sacrifices fine detail and realism. They address this mismatch with a ControlNet training strategy built around consistency training. They also show that the same training principle can produce a unified adapter that improves adaptation of a diffusion model's ControlNet.

The evaluation compares these strategies quantitatively and qualitatively using pretrained text-to-image latent consistency models. Controls include sketches, edge maps, depth, human poses, low-resolution images, and masked images. The findings establish ways to train or adapt conditional controls specifically for consistency models, addressing the image-quality shortcomings observed with direct transfer.
icml-2024-ccm-real-time-controllable-vis.tldr: CCM uses consistency training to add or adapt ControlNet controls for fast text-to-image consistency models.

paragraphs: Clinical prediction models often assume that the same kinds of patient information will be available during training and deployment. In practice, a research dataset may combine several sources, each with different variables, while a deployed model can access only some of them. This paper addresses how to benefit from rich training data under that mismatch.

CLOPPS uses contrastive learning to train encoders that capture information across data sources. Those encoders then support classifiers whose access is restricted to a single source. The central idea is to use relationships available during training to improve the representation used later, even when the deployed classifier receives a narrower view of the patient.

The approach can work with existing outcome classifiers for either cross-sectional records or longitudinal histories. Experiments on two real-world datasets report consistent improvements over strong baselines across several practical scenarios. These findings support cross-source representation learning as a way to improve prediction when deployment cannot provide every source available during training.
icml-2024-contrastive-learning-for-clini.tldr: CLOPPS learns across clinical data sources during training to improve outcome prediction when only one source is available at inference.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves objectives in which one side minimizes while another maximizes. It appears in adversarial training, generative adversarial networks, and robust optimization. Many convergence guarantees for its algorithms assume Lipschitz smoothness, a restriction on how sharply gradients can change. This paper examines what happens when that restriction does not hold.

The authors provide counterexamples showing that existing algorithms can diverge when their smoothness requirement fails, even in some classic minimax problems. They then analyze a relaxed condition called generalized smoothness. Under this setting, they prove convergence for variants of GDA, SGDA, GDmax, and SGDmax, extending the reach of guarantees associated with these basic optimization approaches.

A numerical experiment also evaluates the proposed algorithms. The main contribution is theoretical: it connects convergence analysis to a broader class of objectives than the usual smoothness assumption permits. The result concerns the analyzed algorithm variants in generalized-smooth problems, so it does not imply that arbitrary minimax procedures converge without structural conditions.
icml-2024-delving-into-the-convergence-o.tldr: The paper proves convergence for variants of basic minimax algorithms under generalized smoothness, beyond the usual Lipschitz-smooth setting.

paragraphs: A regression model can produce different output distributions across groups, raising concerns about statistical parity. This paper develops a differentially private procedure that adjusts an existing regressor's outputs to improve fairness. Because it operates through output remapping, the procedure can be applied to any given regressor.

The algorithm first estimates output distributions using histograms, with the Laplace mechanism providing privacy for that estimation. It then computes a Wasserstein barycenter, a shared distribution defined through transport between distributions. Finally, it uses optimal transport maps to move the original outputs toward that common distribution. Aligning distributions in this way is the mechanism used to satisfy the fairness objective.

The authors analyze sample complexity and give a fairness guarantee. Their analysis also exposes a practical choice: how many histogram bins to use. Fewer bins favor fairness but increase error, reflecting a trade-off involving statistical bias and variance. Thus, the distribution-estimation step directly influences the balance between prediction error and fairness in the resulting post-processed model.
icml-2024-differentially-private-post-pr.tldr: The method privately estimates prediction distributions and remaps them toward a shared distribution, with an analyzed fairness–error trade-off.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning helps learn useful representations when task-specific labels are scarce. However, many methods require substantial message passing between connected nodes whenever representations are computed. That inference cost creates a problem for applications with tight response-time requirements. GraphECL aims to retain useful graph information while reducing this deployment burden.

The method couples a graph neural network with a multilayer perceptron, or MLP. The MLP learns to efficiently mimic computations performed by the graph network, allowing inference to proceed without expensive message passing. The authors also provide a theoretical explanation of how an MLP can capture essential information about neighboring structure well enough to match graph-network performance on downstream tasks.

Experiments on widely used real-world benchmarks report better predictive performance and inference efficiency than leading graph contrastive methods. The evaluation includes both homophilous and heterophilous graphs, covering different patterns of similarity among connected nodes. The findings support transferring structural learning into a cheaper inference model as a practical route to faster graph representations.
icml-2024-efficient-contrastive-learning.tldr: GraphECL trains an MLP alongside a graph neural network to produce effective graph representations without message passing at inference.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from multiple clients, creating an opportunity for malicious participants to submit poisoned updates. Defenses based on comparisons across clients can struggle when clients have very different data or many clients are malicious. FedREDefense instead assesses whether an update appears to have resulted from genuine training.

Its central finding concerns reconstruction. Updates produced by genuine training can be approximately reconstructed using some distilled local knowledge, whereas the deliberately handcrafted poisoning updates studied cannot. The defense uses discrepancies in reconstruction error to identify and filter malicious clients. Its assessment relies on characteristics of the update itself, rather than requiring similar client distributions or a predominantly benign client population.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets show successful filtering of model poisoning attacks, including settings with strongly non-identical data distributions and large numbers of malicious clients. The result supports reconstruction error as a useful defense signal in these challenging settings. The stated distinction specifically connects genuine training updates with the handcrafted poisoning behavior examined by the method.
icml-2024-fedredefense-defending-against.tldr: FedREDefense detects poisoned federated-learning updates through reconstruction errors, without relying on similar client data or a benign majority.

paragraphs: Two-stage stochastic programming models decisions under uncertainty by considering possible scenarios. Solving a problem can become expensive when there are many scenarios, so selecting representative ones is a practical shortcut. This paper argues that selection should account for relationships among scenarios and for the order in which selected scenarios reach the solver.

HGCN2SP represents the problem using a hierarchical graph that encodes individual scenarios and their relationships. A hierarchical graph convolutional network extracts features, and an attention-based decoder chooses scenarios in an appropriate order. Reinforcement learning trains this selection policy using feedback from the solver, connecting the learned choices to the behavior of the solution process.

Evaluation on two classic stochastic-programming problems reports high-quality decisions within short computational times. The model also generalizes to larger instances with numbers of variables or scenarios not seen during training. These findings suggest that learning both scenario representation and selection order can make representative-scenario methods useful beyond the instance sizes used to train the policy.
icml-2024-hgcn2sp-hierarchical-graph-con.tldr: HGCN2SP uses hierarchical graph representations and solver feedback to learn which uncertainty scenarios to select and in what order.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions and can serve as surrogates for solutions across a family of partial differential equations. This paper builds an attention-like component from the mathematical structure of those mappings. Its starting point is that a kernel integral operator can be expressed using orthonormal eigenfunctions.

The method represents these eigenfunctions directly with flexible neural networks and uses them to transform the input function according to the integral operator. The resulting module resembles ordinary attention but replaces softmax with an orthogonalization operation. That operation also regularizes training, helping reduce overfitting when data are limited, and can be implemented with little additional computational overhead.

Experiments cover six standard neural-operator benchmarks with both regular and irregular geometries. The authors report that their method can outperform competing baselines by meaningful margins. The contribution links an operator's mathematical representation to an implementable neural module: the same structural choice supplies both the transformation mechanism and a useful source of regularization.
icml-2024-improved-operator-learning-by-.tldr: Orthogonal attention builds neural operators from learned eigenfunctions, using orthogonalization to improve regularization and benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Multi-head attention lets a transformer compute several attention patterns, but its heads operate independently. The paper connects this independence to redundant heads and restrictions on the rank of attention-score matrices. It proposes dynamically composable multi-head attention, or DCMHA, to increase expressive power by allowing heads to be combined according to the input.

At the center is a Compose function that transforms both attention-score matrices and attention-weight matrices in an input-dependent way. The architecture is designed to use parameters and computation efficiently. It can replace ordinary multi-head attention within a transformer, producing the corresponding DCFormer without requiring an entirely new model framework.

Language-modeling experiments span different architectures and model sizes. DCFormer significantly improves on the compared transformers and matches performance associated with models using 1.7 to 2.0 times the compute. One example, DCPythia-6.9B, exceeds Pythia-12B on pretraining perplexity and downstream evaluation. These results support richer interaction among attention heads as a way to improve model performance at a given computational scale.
icml-2024-improving-transformers-with-dy.tldr: DCMHA dynamically combines attention heads based on the input, improving language-model performance with efficient parameter and compute use.

paragraphs: A deployed neural network may be altered after it has been provided as a service. Fingerprinting checks model integrity by submitting specially chosen inputs and examining the responses. IBSF addresses a restrictive black-box setting in which verification can use only the model's top-ranked class label, rather than scores or internal computations.

The method exploits the fact that tampering changes decision boundaries. Starting from normal inputs, it maximizes partial Shannon entropy over a chosen subset of categories. This positions fingerprint inputs near locations where boundaries among those categories intersect, while keeping them almost indistinguishable from their source inputs. Such locations make the returned label sensitive to changes in the model.

The authors theoretically establish and experimentally confirm that expected tampering sensitivity increases as the selected category subset grows. Extensive evaluation reports stronger detection than existing fingerprinting methods, particularly with larger subsets. The result makes boundary intersections a useful design principle for integrity checks that must work with the limited information supplied by top-1 labels.
icml-2024-intersecting-boundary-sensitiv.tldr: IBSF detects model tampering using top-1 labels from fingerprint inputs placed near intersections of multiple class boundaries.

paragraphs: Training transformers with low-precision numbers can reduce cost, but lowering arithmetic precision alone does not guarantee a useful speedup. Existing fully quantized methods often repeatedly quantize, compute, and dequantize. The paper identifies memory-access overhead and inaccurate low-precision computation as reasons this pattern can deliver limited acceleration and degraded transformer performance.

Jetfire combines two changes aimed at those problems. An INT8 data flow optimizes memory access, while per-block quantization helps preserve the accuracy of pretrained transformers. Treating data movement and numerical representation together matters because an efficient low-precision computation can lose its practical advantage when the surrounding data handling remains expensive.

Experiments report accuracy comparable to FP16 training and improvements over existing INT8 transformer-training methods. For a standard transformer block, Jetfire achieves a 1.42-fold end-to-end training speedup and a 1.49-fold memory reduction relative to the FP16 baseline. Those measurements demonstrate the efficiency benefit at the block level, alongside the broader experimental evidence that the training method preserves comparable accuracy.
icml-2024-jetfire-efficient-and-accurate.tldr: Jetfire combines INT8 data flow with per-block quantization to accelerate transformer training while maintaining accuracy comparable to FP16.

paragraphs: When an agent cannot directly observe the full state of its environment, exploration may require deliberately gathering information. Simply visiting more places can miss this need. The paper's example is checking traffic before choosing a route: the useful action reveals something that changes the eventual decision.

The proposed agent receives an exploration bonus for gathering hidden-state information relevant to completing its task. Training therefore requires a way to identify that useful information. It can come from prior knowledge supplied by the user, including privileged information, or from examining complete trajectories in hindsight with off-policy learning. The latter lets later observations reveal what earlier information-gathering actions accomplished.

Experiments across partially observed environments show performance competitive with prior methods when little exploration is needed and substantially better performance when complex exploration strategies are required. The agent also learns without privileged information by using whole trajectories retrospectively. These findings support rewarding task-relevant information acquisition as a way to teach purposeful exploration under partial observation.
icml-2024-learning-to-explore-in-pomdps-.tldr: The method rewards task-relevant information gathering to teach exploration strategies in partially observed environments, including through hindsight without privileged information.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuning collections contain examples for many abilities, while an application may need a particular skill. LESS addresses targeted instruction tuning: choosing the examples most useful for developing that capability. A few examples of the desired behavior provide the target against which candidate training data are assessed.

The method builds a reusable datastore of low-dimensional gradient features and searches for training examples with similar features to the target examples. These gradients describe training-related behavior rather than just textual resemblance. LESS adapts influence estimation to the Adam optimizer and to variable-length instruction examples, making the selection procedure better suited to the actual tuning process.

Experiments show that a selected five percent of the data can often outperform full-dataset training across downstream tasks. Selections also transfer from smaller to larger models and across model families. Qualitative analysis indicates that the method can identify relevant reasoning skills beyond surface wording. Together, these findings support influence-based selection as a practical way to concentrate tuning on a desired capability.
icml-2024-less-selecting-influential-dat.tldr: LESS selects instruction-tuning data through optimizer-aware gradient similarity, often letting a five-percent subset outperform full-data training on targeted tasks.

paragraphs: Some approaches to large traveling salesman problems use a learned heatmap to guide Monte Carlo tree search. The heatmap estimates which edges belong in an optimal tour, and search uses those estimates to construct solutions. This position paper examines whether the learned component and the combined search paradigm deliver the value attributed to them.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental analysis questioning machine-learning-based heatmap generation. They demonstrate that a simple baseline can outperform complex learned approaches at this stage. They also compare the broader heatmap-guided search paradigm with LKH-3 and find it inferior, despite its use of problem-specific, handcrafted strategies.

These findings challenge both the contribution of learned heatmaps and the practical competitiveness of the surrounding pipeline in the studied setting. The paper proposes two directions: stronger theoretical foundations for heatmap generation and more autonomous, generalizable machine-learning approaches to combinatorial problems. Its argument encourages separating gains from the learned guidance from those supplied by search and handcrafted components.
icml-2024-position-rethinking-post-hoc-s.tldr: The paper challenges learned heatmap-guided TSP search, finding a simple heatmap baseline competitive and the overall paradigm inferior to LKH-3.

paragraphs: A machine that rates images or videos should produce judgments aligned with human opinion. Q-Align studies how to teach that ability to large multimodal models. Its starting observation is that people in subjective rating studies learn and use discrete levels described in words, rather than learning to assign unrestricted numerical scores directly.

The method therefore trains models with text-defined rating levels. This changes how the task is taught while retaining the original multimodal model structure. The same teaching approach is also used to combine image quality assessment, image aesthetic assessment, and video quality assessment into a single model called OneAlign.

Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy for Q-Align across all three assessment tasks and show an advantage for discrete-level training over direct-score training. The models can also provide effective evaluations finer than the levels used to teach them. This means a coarse verbal training scale need not force equally coarse output judgments, making the choice of supervision format central to the paper's contribution.
icml-2024-q-align-teaching-lmms-for-visu.tldr: Q-Align improves visual assessment by teaching multimodal models text-defined rating levels, while still enabling finer-grained evaluations.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small subset of training data chosen so that a model trained on it performs comparably to one trained on the full dataset. This paper focuses on a practical question within that idea: how small can the subset become while still meeting a model-performance requirement? It formulates this as refined coreset selection.

The proposed method jointly handles performance and subset size while maintaining an explicit priority order between them. Model performance takes priority, and coreset size is optimized within that ordering. This gives the search a direct connection to the practitioner's objective of reducing training cost while preserving a required level of predictive performance.

The authors establish a convergence guarantee for their method and evaluate it experimentally against previous strategies. They report that it often finds smaller subsets with better model performance. The finding supports treating subset size as something to optimize under a performance constraint, rather than assuming the desired data reduction must be settled independently of the resulting model quality.
icml-2024-refined-coreset-selection-towa.tldr: Refined coreset selection searches for smaller training subsets while prioritizing model-performance constraints, often improving both size and performance experimentally.

paragraphs: GANs can struggle with diverse data whose underlying structure is complex. This paper identifies a specific weakness in their usual adversarial objective: it is insufficient to correct generated regions of positive measure that lie outside the real-data manifold. The issue concerns substantial regions of generated outputs, rather than merely isolated problematic points.

SMaRt adds score-matching regularity to GAN optimization. The motivation is that a score function can keep pushing generated points toward the real-data manifold. A toy experiment uses a known ground-truth score to demonstrate more accurate reproduction of the data distribution. For real-world datasets, pretrained diffusion models provide approximate score functions.

The experiments report consistent synthesis improvements across several state-of-the-art GANs. For Aurora trained on ImageNet at 64 by 64 resolution, FID improves from 8.87 to 7.11, matching the reported performance of a one-step consistency model. These findings connect the theoretical weakness in adversarial training with a concrete supplementary signal that improves the tested generators.
icml-2024-smart-improving-gans-with-scor.tldr: SMaRt supplements GAN training with score-matching regularity, using diffusion-model scores to improve generated samples in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks compute through sparse events whose timing can carry information. This paper investigates whether that temporal structure can support reasoning over concepts and relations in graphs, including knowledge graphs. The central question is how to make timing useful for relation processing rather than treating spikes only as a different computational format.

The approach combines temporal coding with synaptic delays. Through a neural-generalized path formulation, spike timing becomes an additional dimension for encoding properties of relations. Delays therefore play a role in how relational information is processed as part of graph reasoning. This connects a distinctive feature of spiking computation directly to the structure of the reasoning task.

Empirical results show the usefulness of temporal delays and strong performance across diverse graph-reasoning tasks. The authors also theoretically estimate a twentyfold energy saving relative to non-spiking counterparts. That energy figure is an estimate, while the task-performance findings are experimental. Together, they motivate further use of temporal spiking mechanisms for efficient relational computation.
icml-2024-temporal-spiking-neural-networ.tldr: The paper uses spike timing and synaptic delays to encode graph relations, reporting strong reasoning results and theoretically estimated energy savings.

paragraphs: AI weather forecasts still need an initial estimate of the atmosphere, usually produced through traditional data assimilation. Four-dimensional variational assimilation, or 4DVar, is accurate but computationally expensive. FengWu-4DVar combines the FengWu forecasting model with this assimilation process to create a framework that produces its own analysis states for forecasting.

The framework embeds FengWu and a representation of its errors into the 4DVar objective. It uses a spherical-harmonic approximation to capture horizontal correlations in background error, and automatic differentiation to determine the optimized analysis fields. These components connect the learned forecasting model to the process that prepares its starting conditions.

Tests use simulated observations derived from ERA5 with different observation proportions and noise levels. The framework produces accurate analysis fields and sustains stable, self-contained global forecasting for a full year in that setting. It is also approximately one hundred times faster than traditional 4DVar under similar experimental conditions. These results demonstrate computational promise while grounding the forecast claim in simulated-observation experiments.
icml-2024-towards-a-self-contained-data-.tldr: FengWu-4DVar integrates AI forecasting with data assimilation, sustaining year-long forecasting in simulated-observation tests with substantially faster assimilation.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates network design, but the search space creates a trade-off. A narrow space can exclude architectures needed for some tasks, while a broad one can make searching expensive. This paper uses a hierarchy of generative models to navigate an extremely large, general-purpose architecture space efficiently.

The first level uses a conditional continuous normalizing flow to design micro-cells, the smaller architectural components. The second uses a transformer-based sequence generator to assemble macro architectures that reflect task needs and architectural constraints. This divides architecture generation into the design of components and the organization of the larger network.

To keep the process computationally feasible, the generators are pretrained without a specific target task using a metric space based on graph similarities and zero-cost similarities between architectures. Experiments report state-of-the-art results among low-cost architecture-search methods across CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and NAS-Bench-360. The findings support hierarchical generation as a way to make a broad architecture space accessible without giving up computational efficiency.
icml-2024-towards-neural-architecture-se.tldr: A two-level generative hierarchy designs network components and full architectures to search a broad space efficiently.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for reasoning faces a supervision problem: a reward for the final answer says little about where an incorrect solution went wrong. Rewarding individual steps offers more guidance but requires substantial annotation. R³ uses correct demonstrations to extract step-level learning benefits while relying only on outcome supervision.

Training begins near the end of a correct demonstration, where the model has relatively little reasoning left to complete. The starting point then moves progressively toward the demonstration's beginning. This reverse curriculum makes exploration easier at successive stages and allows final-outcome feedback to provide signals about particular portions of the reasoning process, helping locate errors.

With Llama2-7B, the method exceeds the reported reinforcement-learning baseline by an average of 4.1 points across eight reasoning tasks. In program-based reasoning, seven-billion-parameter models trained with R³ perform comparably to larger or closed-source models. These results support using the structure of correct demonstrations to make sparse outcome rewards more informative, without introducing manually annotated rewards for every reasoning step.
icml-2024-training-large-language-models.tldr: R³ starts reasoning practice near the end of correct demonstrations and works backward, making outcome-only rewards more useful for learning.

paragraphs: In crowdsourced multi-label learning, an example can have several true labels, but training receives unreliable annotations from different people. Earlier inference approaches require crowdsourced labels for both training and test examples. This paper instead studies learning a predictive model from noisy training annotations, making prediction the central objective.

The authors model how crowdsourced labels are generated using transition matrices and derive an unbiased estimator of prediction risk. They then aggregate annotations and transition matrices across annotators to make matrix estimation easier while preserving the estimator's theoretical properties. A decoupled autoencoder framework additionally exploits relationships among labels to improve performance.

The paper supplies a generalization-error bound supporting convergence of the empirical risk estimator and reports effective results across several crowdsourced multi-label scenarios. The contribution combines a theoretically grounded correction for unreliable supervision with a model that uses label correlations. This addresses both the annotation-noise problem and the fact that multiple labels on the same example can carry useful information about one another.
icml-2024-unbiased-multi-label-learning-.tldr: The method combines an unbiased risk estimator for crowdsourced label noise with a framework that exploits correlations among multiple labels.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can suffer from robust overfitting: performance on adversarial test examples deteriorates as training continues. Earlier stability analyses connect this behavior to the lack of uniform stability in SGD-based adversarial training. This paper develops an algorithm designed to obtain that stability, addressing the optimization process behind the observed problem.

ME-A uses a Moreau envelope function to reformulate the objective as a problem with two nested minimizations. The reformulation separates the adversarial loss's non-smoothness from its lack of strong convexity. The algorithm alternates between the inner and outer minimization problems and achieves uniform stability without additional computational overhead, according to the paper.

Practical experiments demonstrate mitigation of robust overfitting. The theoretical contribution also extends beyond adversarial training: the authors identify ME-A as the first uniformly stable algorithm for weakly convex, non-smooth problems. The experimental finding concerns reducing robust overfitting, while the broader result concerns stability for this specified mathematical class of objectives; these are related but distinct contributions.
icml-2024-uniformly-stable-algorithms-fo.tldr: ME-A uses a Moreau-envelope reformulation to achieve uniform stability for weakly convex, non-smooth optimization and mitigate robust overfitting.
